name: Grace Abbott

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm in by half seven at Calloway Building Supply, where I buy timber, fixings, insulation and plasterboard for the builders' merchants we serve. My day is a paper notebook, two phones and a lot of tea. I check what's coming in on the lorries, ring the mills about delays, and argue with Gareth (our sales director) about what we can afford to hold. I like that it's real stuff: you can walk out to the yard and see it. What wears me out is the swings. A wet spring, a rate rise, and nobody builds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so, and then go back to my tea. At work I'd say it was a lot of fuss over a better spreadsheet. To friends I'd say good, nothing to worry about, and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I carry on, which suits me fine. I never trusted the hype. My real worries are the usual: building slowing down, the mortgage, and Holly's school fees for the secondary she wants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am. Notebook, phones, calls with the mills on Monday mornings. I'd put maybe 200 a month extra aside for the mortgage, as the base rate worries me more than any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled. Not thrilled, because I'm already tense about the market, but nothing about AI would add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said building can stall after a rate rise. Is that still a worry in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, always. If the building market stalls for six months, I'd be holding too much stock and Gareth would be on at me. It's the cycle that frightens me, not computers. I've lived through two downturns and I remember them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the younger buyers about how you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them that you learn the mills by talking to them. A mill in trouble tells you in the tone of its voice, and a screen can't hear that.

say: It was a lot of **fuss** over a better spreadsheet.
Nothing to worry about, so I'll go back to my **tea**.
think: My **real worries** are the building cycle, the mortgage and the school fees Holly will need.
I never trusted the **hype**, and I'm glad I didn't.
do: Carry on with the notebook, two phones and Monday calls with the **mills**.
Put **200 a month** extra aside because the base rate worries me.
feel: **Settled**, but already tense about the building market.
S0.quote: A mill in trouble tells you in the tone of its voice, and a screen can't hear that.
fieldNote: Grace's **resistance** is stubborn but grounded in what has worked for her.
Her main worry is the **building cycle**, which she'd call the real threat.

steps.text: Keep the Monday morning calls with every mill
Set aside 200 a month towards the mortgage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's see it work before we bet on it. To friends I'd say sensible people wait. Online I wouldn't say anything, because it's full of shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's coming for the junior desk jobs first. The two young buyers do price comparisons and stock checks, and a program can do that. It won't do my calls, but I'm not fool enough to think nobody would notice. They might ask why we need a senior buyer if the juniors go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and watch. I'd see how Gareth and the board handle it, and I'd talk to the builders' merchants we sell to, as they'll tell me what they want. I'd keep building the supplier relationships, since that's the part that's hard to copy. If it comes to it, I'd ask for a move towards key accounts, where it's people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. There's a part of me that dislikes being told to learn something I've managed without for twenty years. That's stubbornness, I know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your team is most exposed if software does the buying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ollie and Marsha, the two juniors on my desk. They do the comparison work and they'd see their days change first. I'd feel responsible, because I'd be the one to tell them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If tools do get proven, what would change your mind about using them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a tool made fewer mistakes than I do, and I could check it, I'd use it. Not before. I've been burned by sales demos, and I don't want to be the guinea pig.

say: Let's see it **work** before we bet on it.
Sensible people **wait** until a tool has proved itself, and I won't be the first to try.
think: The **junior** desk jobs go first, and then someone may ask why we need a senior buyer.
My calls with mills are hard to copy, but I'm not **fooled** into thinking nobody would notice.
do: Wait and watch how Gareth and the board handle it, and ask **customers** what they want.
Ask for a move towards **key accounts**, where it's people, if it comes to it.
feel: **Uneasy**, with some stubbornness about being told to learn.
S1.quote: I've been burned by sales demos, and I don't want to be the guinea pig.
fieldNote: Grace's **resistance** is honest: she'd use a tool only when it's proven and checkable.
She feels **responsible** for the juniors Ollie and Marsha, which shapes her worry.

steps.text: Watch how the board handles the first tools
Ask the builders' merchants what they want
Ask for a move to key accounts if desk jobs shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say we need a plan, now, and I'd ask the board what it is. To friends I'd say sit tight and look after your money. Online I'd say governments are asleep, and somebody has to wake them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm rattled. Even I can see a machine doing what a buyer does, and doing it overnight. It's the speed that gets me. Two years is nothing: it's barely time to finish a house extension. I don't know what Calloway would do with a senior buyer at that point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut spending straight away, with no holiday this year, and the car stays another three years. I'd move cash into the safe account and put the mortgage overpayment up. I'd talk to Gareth about whether any role survives. And I'd probably find out what my pension is worth, which I've avoided looking at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be sleeping badly, and I'd be short with the children, which I'd hate. I'm someone who likes to know the plan, and there wouldn't be one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Neil that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Neil (my husband, a quantity surveyor) that we have savings and that we aren't going to panic. He works with sites and people, so he has more time than I do. Maybe that's the one comfort I'd cling to. Then I'd say, let's not tell the children until we know more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of this scares you more, the speed or the size?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The speed. The size is what it is, because we'll all adapt in the end. But two years doesn't give Calloway, or the government, or us, time to turn around. A slow train is easier to get off than a fast one, and two years is a very fast train.

say: We need a **plan** now, and I'd ask the board what it is.
Governments are **asleep**, and somebody has to wake them.
think: I'm **rattled**: a machine could do a buyer's job overnight, and two years is nothing.
I don't know what Calloway would do with a senior buyer, and I'm not sure I want to **know**.
do: Cut spending: no **holiday**, keep the car three more years, and raise mortgage overpayments.
Ask Gareth whether any **role** survives, and finally check what my pension is worth.
feel: **Anxious**, sleeping badly and short with the children.
S2.quote: A slow train is easier to get off than a fast one, and two years is a very fast train.
fieldNote: Grace's **resistance** leaves her without a ready plan, which is why her anxiety is high despite savings.
Neil's site-based job gives her **a little** more time, though she doesn't count on it.

steps.text: Cancel this year's holiday and keep the car three more years
Move spare cash into the safe account
Ask Gareth whether any buying role survives
Check what my pension is worth

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say let's not rush, but let's not sleep on it either. To friends I'd say start putting money aside. Online I'd say the government should say what its plan is, since five years is a short time for a country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is workable. I'm 43 now, so I'd be 48. That's an awkward age to start over, but it's possible. I'm wary, but not panicking, and I think the ones who prepare will be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd finally get over myself and try one of these tools in a small way, just to know what I'm up against. I'd put away a third of my pay and pay down the mortgage. I'd also look at moving to key accounts or a role training new people, anything where the human part stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wary. There's a determination in it, more than the other one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first of those five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, in the end. I'd use them in year one or two, because I'd want to understand it, not because I like it. If I'm going to be told what it can do, I'd rather know with my own eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would five years make you try the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Gareth in year one, not year four, about what the company needs. I'd say I'm happy to move to a role where I deal with suppliers and customers in person, and I'd like him to say what that looks like. If he can't, I'd start looking round.

say: Let's not rush, but **don't sleep** on it either.
The government should say its **plan**, because five years is short for a country.
think: I'd be **48**, an awkward age to start over, but possible.
The ones who **prepare** will be fine.
do: Try one tool in year one **just** to know what I'm up against.
Save a **third of my pay** and ask Gareth about a role that keeps the human part.
feel: **Wary**, but with more determination than in the two-year version.
S3.quote: If I'm going to be told what it can do, I'd rather know with my own eyes.
fieldNote: Grace is still **resistant**, but five years makes her willing to try one tool to see for herself.
She'd **ask Gareth early** rather than wait, which shows her pragmatism.

steps.text: Try one buying tool in a small way
Save a third of my pay and pay down the mortgage
Ask Gareth in year one about a people-facing role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say nothing, honestly, because ten years sounds like someone else's problem. To friends I'd say it's far enough off to plan. Online I'd say have an honest chat about it, and don't scare people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be 53. I'd probably have done the job for a long time and maybe be ready for something calmer. It's a long way off, and a lot can change, including the AI not getting there. I'm more worried about my children's jobs than mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am for a few years and pay off the mortgage faster. I'd try a tool around year three, once it's proven. I'd keep up my supplier relationships and perhaps train the younger buyers in the people side. And I'd help Holly and Ben choose studies, probably something practical and hands-on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm enough. A bit sad, as I like the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too far away to feel real?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, it feels unreal, and that's the risk. I know I'd put it off. Ten years feels unreal, and that's the risk, so I'd set myself a date to look at it again. Say the Easter of year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have done by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By year five I'd want the mortgage nearly cleared, a good savings pot, and a plan for what comes next. I'd also want to be doing something where my knowledge counts for something, like training people or running key accounts.

say: Ten years sounds like someone else's problem, but it's far enough off to **plan**.
Have an honest chat about it, and **don't scare** people.
think: I'd be **53**, maybe ready for something calmer, and the AI might not even get there.
I'm more worried about my **children's** jobs than mine.
do: Pay off the **mortgage** faster and try a proven tool around year three.
Train younger buyers in the **people side** and help my children pick practical studies.
feel: **Calm** enough, with a bit of sadness, as I like the job.
S4.quote: Ten years feels unreal, and that's the risk, so I'd set myself a date to look at it again.
fieldNote: Grace is **calm** because ten years gives her time and her cushion is strong.
She knows she'd **procrastinate**, so she sets herself a date to look again.

steps.text: Pay off the mortgage faster over five years
Try a proven tool around year three
Train younger buyers in the people side of buying
Guide Holly and Ben towards practical studies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's the speed that does it, because nobody has a plan, least of all me. What would help is a clear message from the government and from Calloway about what's coming, some money for retraining that's real, and time. Even one more year would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people like me are called stubborn when we're just careful. I'm not against change, I just want to see it work before I bet my family on it.

headlineQuote: I'm not against change, I just want to see it work before I bet my family on it.
portrait: Grace is a 43-year-old senior **building materials buyer** at Calloway Building Supply, with a husband, two children and a mortgage.
She is centrist and **resistant**: notebook, phones and calls with the mills, and she won't try a tool until it's proven.
Her mood is uneasy in gentle worlds, **anxious** when AGI is near, and calm again with ten years to plan.
She feels **responsible** for her junior buyers and worries about her children's jobs.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario, because the speed leaves no time for Calloway, government or her family.
whatWouldHelp: A clear **plan** from government and employer, real retraining money, and more time.
